[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Database Normalization (1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF)"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Database normalization is the process of organizing data in a database to reduce redundancy and improve data integrity. It involves dividing databases into tables and defining relationships between the tables. The goal is to isolate data so that amendments to an attribute are made in only one table. This tutorial covers the first four normal forms: 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, and BCNF (Boyce-Codd Normal Form)."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Why Normalize?"},{"order":4,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Minimize data redundancy: Reduces storage space and avoids inconsistencies."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Improve data integrity: Ensures data is accurate and consistent."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Simplify data modification: Makes it easier to update, insert, and delete data."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Enhance query performance: Well-structured data leads to faster query execution."},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"1NF (First Normal Form)"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"A table is in 1NF if it contains only atomic values (i.e., each column contains only one value) and there are no repeating groups of columns. In other words, each attribute should contain only a single value, and each record needs to be unique."},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"Consider a table named 'Orders' that is not in 1NF:"},{"order":11,"type":"code","text":"Order ID | Customer ID | Products
------- | -------- | --------
1 | 101 | ProductA, ProductB
2 | 102 | ProductC
3 | 101 | ProductD, ProductE, ProductF"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"The 'Products' column contains multiple values. To convert this to 1NF, we create separate rows for each product:"},{"order":13,"type":"code","text":"Order ID | Customer ID | Product
------- | -------- | --------
1 | 101 | ProductA
1 | 101 | ProductB
2 | 102 | ProductC
3 | 101 | ProductD
3 | 101 | ProductE
3 | 101 | ProductF"},{"order":14,"type":"subheading","text":"2NF (Second Normal Form)"},{"order":15,"type":"paragraph","text":"A table is in 2NF if it is in 1NF and all non-key attributes are fully functionally dependent on the primary key. This means that every non-key attribute must depend on the entire primary key, not just part of it. 2NF is only relevant if the primary key is a composite key (i.e., made up of two or more attributes)."},{"order":16,"type":"paragraph","text":"Consider the following table:"},{"order":17,"type":"code","text":"Order ID | Product ID | Product Name | Quantity | Order Date
------- | -------- | -------- | -------- | --------
1 | 1 | Laptop | 1 | 2023-01-01
1 | 2 | Mouse | 2 | 2023-01-01
2 | 1 | Laptop | 1 | 2023-01-05
3 | 3 | Keyboard | 1 | 2023-01-10"},{"order":18,"type":"paragraph","text":"Here, the primary key is a composite key: (Order ID, Product ID). 'Product Name' depends only on 'Product ID', not on the entire primary key. 'Quantity' and 'Order Date' depend on the entire primary key. To achieve 2NF, we split the table into two:"},{"order":19,"type":"code","text":"Orders Table:
Order ID | Product ID | Quantity | Order Date
------- | -------- | -------- | --------
1 | 1 | 1 | 2023-01-01
1 | 2 | 2 | 2023-01-01
2 | 1 | 1 | 2023-01-05
3 | 3 | 1 | 2023-01-10

Products Table:
Product ID | Product Name
------- | --------
1 | Laptop
2 | Mouse
3 | Keyboard"},{"order":20,"type":"subheading","text":"3NF (Third Normal Form)"},{"order":21,"type":"paragraph","text":"A table is in 3NF if it is in 2NF and no non-key attribute is transitively dependent on the primary key. Transitive dependency means that a non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute. In other words, all non-key attributes must depend directly on the primary key."},{"order":22,"type":"paragraph","text":"Consider the following 'Employees' table:"},{"order":23,"type":"code","text":"Employee ID | Employee Name | Department ID | Department Name | Location
------- | -------- | -------- | -------- | --------
1 | John Doe | 101 | Sales | New York
2 | Jane Smith | 102 | Marketing | London
3 | Peter Jones | 101 | Sales | New York"},{"order":24,"type":"paragraph","text":"Here, 'Department Name' and 'Location' depend on 'Department ID', which is a non-key attribute. This is a transitive dependency. To achieve 3NF, we split the table into two:"},{"order":25,"type":"code","text":"Employees Table:
Employee ID | Employee Name | Department ID
------- | -------- | --------
1 | John Doe | 101
2 | Jane Smith | 102
3 | Peter Jones | 101

Departments Table:
Department ID | Department Name | Location
------- | -------- | --------
101 | Sales | New York
102 | Marketing | London"},{"order":26,"type":"subheading","text":"BCNF (Boyce-Codd Normal Form)"},{"order":27,"type":"paragraph","text":"BCNF is a stronger version of 3NF. A table is in BCNF if every determinant is a candidate key. A determinant is any attribute (or set of attributes) that determines another attribute. In simpler terms, for every dependency A -> B, A must be a candidate key. BCNF addresses situations where 3NF is insufficient, particularly when there are overlapping candidate keys."},{"order":28,"type":"paragraph","text":"Consider the following 'Courses' table:"},{"order":29,"type":"code","text":"Course | Teacher | Textbook
------- | -------- | --------
Database | Dr. Smith | SQL Guide
Database | Dr. Jones | SQL Guide
Operating Systems | Dr. Brown | OS Concepts"},{"order":30,"type":"paragraph","text":"Assume the following dependencies:
1.  A course determines the textbook used (Course -> Textbook).
2.  A textbook determines the course (Textbook -> Course).
3.  A teacher can teach multiple courses, and a course can be taught by multiple teachers.

In this case, both 'Course' and 'Textbook' are candidate keys. However, 'Teacher' is not a candidate key, and 'Textbook -> Course' violates BCNF because 'Textbook' is a determinant, but not a superkey."},{"order":31,"type":"paragraph","text":"To achieve BCNF, we split the table into two:"},{"order":32,"type":"code","text":"CourseTextbooks Table:
Course | Textbook
------- | --------
Database | SQL Guide
Operating Systems | OS Concepts

TeacherCourse Table:
Teacher | Course
------- | --------
Dr. Smith | Database
Dr. Jones | Database
Dr. Brown | Operating Systems"},{"order":33,"type":"subheading","text":"Conclusion"},{"order":34,"type":"paragraph","text":"Database normalization is a crucial aspect of database design. By following the normal forms (1NF, 2NF, 3NF, and BCNF), you can create databases that are efficient, consistent, and easy to maintain. While higher normal forms exist (4NF, 5NF, etc.), 3NF and BCNF are often sufficient for most practical applications. Remember to consider the trade-offs between normalization and performance, as excessive normalization can sometimes lead to more complex queries."}]
